section.title: Abraham Justified by Faith
section.sectionRationale: Having declared in chapter 3 that God justifies sinners freely by grace through faith apart from works of the law, Paul now proves it from the Scriptures using the towering example of Abraham. If anyone could have boasted before God, it was the father of the Jewish nation; yet Genesis says Abraham believed God and it was credited to him as righteousness. Paul shows that this crediting came by faith and not by works, before circumcision and before the law, so that Abraham is the father of all who believe, Jew and Gentile alike. The chapter climbs to a full portrait of saving faith: against all hope Abraham believed in hope, fully convinced that God could do what He had promised, and closes by turning that same faith toward us who trust the God who raised Jesus.
section.thesis: Abraham was justified not by works but by faith, credited as righteousness before he was circumcised and apart from the law, so that he is the father of all who believe; and the same righteousness is credited to all who trust in the God who raised Jesus, who was delivered over for our trespasses and raised for our justification.
section.frameNote: Four movements: Abraham credited righteous by faith and not by works; the blessing given before circumcision so that he fathers Jew and Gentile; the promise received through faith and not law; and the portrait of Abraham's faith against hope, applied to us who believe in Him who raised Jesus.

units.label: Credited by faith, not works
units.note: Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him

verses.text: What then shall we say that Abraham, our forefather according to the flesh, has discovered?
If Abraham was indeed justified by works, he had something to boast about, but not before God.
For what does the Scripture say? “Abraham believed God, and it was {{logizomai|credited}} to him as {{dikaiosyne|righteousness}}.”
Now the wages of the worker are not credited as a gift, but as an obligation.
However, to the one who does not work, but believes in Him who justifies the ungodly, his {{pistis|faith}} is credited as righteousness.
And David speaks likewise of the blessedness of the man to whom God credits righteousness apart from works:
“Blessed are they whose lawless acts are forgiven, whose sins are covered.
Blessed is the man whose sin the Lord will never count against him.”
Is this blessing only on the circumcised, or also on the uncircumcised? We have been saying that Abraham’s faith was credited to him as righteousness.
In what context was it credited? Was it after his circumcision, or before? It was not after, but before.

And he received the sign of circumcision as a seal of the righteousness that he had by faith while he was still uncircumcised. So then, he is the father of all who believe but are not circumcised, in order that righteousness might be credited to them.
And he is also the father of the circumcised who not only are circumcised, but who also walk in the footsteps of the faith that our father Abraham had before he was circumcised.

units.label: The promise through faith, not law
units.note: so that it may rest on grace

verses.text: For the promise to Abraham and his offspring that he would be heir of the world was not given through the law, but through the righteousness that comes by faith.
For if those who live by the law are heirs, faith is useless and the promise is worthless,
because the law brings wrath. And where there is no law, there is no transgression.

Therefore, the promise comes by faith, so that it may rest on grace and may be guaranteed to all Abraham’s offspring, not only to those who are of the law, but also to those who are of the faith of Abraham. He is the father of us all.

As it is written: “I have made you a father of many nations.” He is our father in the presence of God, in whom he believed, the God who gives life to the dead and calls into being what does not yet exist.

units.label: Against hope, believing in hope
units.note: fully persuaded God could do what He promised

verses.text: Against all hope, Abraham in {{elpis|hope}} believed and so became the father of many nations, just as he had been told, “So shall your offspring be.”
Without weakening in his faith, he acknowledged the decrepitness of his body (since he was about a hundred years old) and the lifelessness of Sarah’s womb.
Yet he did not waver through disbelief in the promise of God, but was strengthened in his faith and gave glory to God,
being fully persuaded that God was able to do what He had promised.
This is why “it was credited to him as righteousness.”
Now the words “it was credited to him” were written not only for Abraham,
but also for us, to whom righteousness will be credited, for us who believe in Him who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead.
He was delivered over to death for our trespasses and was raised to life for our justification.

logizomai.gloss: To reckon, count, credit, or put to one's account. It is an accounting and legal word, used eleven times in this chapter, describing how God enters righteousness on the ledger of the one who believes. Crucially, the righteousness credited is not the believer's own achievement but a gift reckoned to him; God counts the ungodly righteous on the ground of faith, not works, exactly as Genesis 15:6 says of Abraham.

dikaiosyne.gloss: Righteousness, the state of being right with God, of standing acquitted before His court. In Romans this righteousness is God's own gift, revealed in the gospel and received by faith. Abraham's righteousness was not earned by his works but credited to him when he believed, so that the standing he had before God came from outside himself, from God's reckoning.

pistis.gloss: Faith, trust, reliance. Justifying faith is not a work that earns a wage but the empty hand that receives what God freely gives. Paul sets faith and works in sharp contrast: the worker is paid an obligation, but the believer, who does not work but trusts Him who justifies the ungodly, has faith itself credited as righteousness. Faith looks away from self to the promising God.

elpis.gloss: Hope, confident expectation grounded in God's promise. Abraham's faith is shown as hope against hope: with his own body as good as dead and Sarah's womb barren, he had no natural reason to expect a son, yet he hoped in the God who gives life to the dead. Biblical hope is not wishful thinking but settled assurance resting on the character and word of God.

basic.context: Paul has just argued that God justifies sinners freely by grace through faith, apart from works of the law, so that no one can boast. Now he anticipates the obvious objection: what about Abraham, the father of the Jewish people? Surely he was accepted for his obedience. Paul answers by going to the Scripture itself. Genesis says Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness. That single sentence proves justification is by faith, not works, and it was written for our sake as much as his.
basic.hermeneutics: This chapter is a sustained exposition of one verse, Genesis 15:6, backed by Psalm 32. Read it as a courtroom and accounting argument. The key word credited, or reckoned, appears again and again. Paul reasons about timing (before circumcision), about basis (faith not law), and about scope (Jew and Gentile), and then paints faith itself in the portrait of Abraham. The whole chapter aims to show that the way Abraham was justified is exactly the way we are.
basic.originalLanguages: The chapter turns on logizomai, to credit or reckon, an accounting term for entering righteousness on a person's account. That righteousness is dikaiosyne, a right standing before God, given not earned. It is received by pistis, faith, the trust that does not work for a wage but receives a gift. And Abraham's faith is elpis, hope against hope, confident that the life-giving God would keep His word.
basic.typology: Abraham is more than an example; he is the pattern father of a worldwide family of faith. The promise that he would be father of many nations reaches its fulfillment as Gentiles come to share his faith. The God who brought life from Abraham's dead body and Sarah's barren womb is the same God who raised Jesus from the dead, so Abraham's story foreshadows the resurrection at the heart of the gospel.
basic.christ: The chapter ends at the cross and the empty tomb. The same faith that justified Abraham now rests on Him who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead. Jesus was delivered over for our trespasses and raised for our justification, so the righteousness credited to believers is grounded in His death and resurrection. Abraham believed the promise; we believe the promise kept in Christ.
basic.god: God is the one who justifies the ungodly, who credits righteousness apart from works, who gives life to the dead and calls into being what does not exist. He is a promising God who keeps His word across the centuries, and a gracious God who accepts sinners on the basis of faith so that salvation rests entirely on His grace and not on human achievement.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 15:6 is the seed text: Abraham believed the LORD, and it was counted to him as righteousness. Psalm 32:1-2 adds David's testimony to the blessedness of forgiven sin. Galatians 3 makes the same argument, that those of faith are Abraham's children. James 2 speaks of faith proven by works, a complement not a contradiction.
basic.oneStory: God promised Abraham a family as numerous as the stars, and Abraham simply believed, and was counted righteous. The rest of the Bible unfolds that promise until it opens to all nations in Christ. The God who raised life from a barren womb finally raised Jesus from the grave, and everyone who trusts Him is counted righteous and welcomed into Abraham's worldwide family.

context.literary:
Romans 4 is the proof text for chapter 3. Paul closed 3:31 with a promise that faith upholds the law, and chapter 4 keeps it by putting the Law itself, the book of Genesis, on the witness stand. The whole chapter hangs on one quotation, Genesis 15:6, which is brought in at verse 3 and returned to at verses 9, 22 and 23. Between those returns Paul sets four movements: the basis of Abraham's standing, verses 1 to 8; its timing, verses 9 to 12; its scope, verses 13 to 17; and the nature of the faith itself, verses 18 to 22. Verses 23 to 25 then turn the story around and aim it at the reader.

The chapter is held together by a single accounting verb, logizomai, which appears eleven times between verses 3 and 24. It is the word of the ledger. Paul sets wages against a gift in verse 4, a debt against grace, and then applies the ledger to forgiveness, so that 'credited' in verse 6 and 'count against' in verse 8 are mirror images. The sinner whose sin is not counted and the believer whose faith is counted as righteousness are the same person seen from two sides.

Notice also the way Paul uses two witnesses. Abraham, the Law's great figure, and David, the Psalms' great king, both testify. That fits the standard Jewish pattern that a matter is confirmed by two witnesses, and it implies that the Law and the Writings agree. The promise of fatherhood is bound up in verse 17, which quotes Genesis 17:5, and in verse 18, which quotes Genesis 15:5. Paul has laced the two Genesis scenes together so that the promise and the faith are read as one.
context.historical:
Paul's readers lived in a world in which Abraham was the property of anyone who claimed descent from him. Jewish writings of the period praised him as the model of faithfulness under testing. Sirach 44 describes him as one who kept the law of the Most High, and 1 Maccabees 2:52 asks whether Abraham was not found faithful in testing and so reckoned righteous. In that tradition the verse about believing and being credited could slide toward the idea that his faith was itself a work of loyalty that earned reward. Paul's opening question, 'what has Abraham discovered?', puts the issue plainly: what did the father of the nation obtain, and on what footing?

The matter was far from academic in Rome. The congregation had Jews who regarded circumcision as the entrance to God's people and Gentiles who had never been circumcised. Circumcision had been the mark of Abraham's household since Genesis 17:10-11, and for many it made the difference between a member and an outsider. By arguing that the credit came while Abraham was still uncircumcised, Paul removes the ground from anyone who would make the rite a condition for full standing.

The chapter also has Gentile hearers in view. Abraham came from Ur and Haran, out of an idolatrous background, and his call in Genesis 12:2-3 included a promise that all families of the earth would be blessed. The first Roman Christians would have recognised in this that the covenant had always been aimed at the nations. Paul's argument is not a reversal of the Jewish story but a recovery of its original scope.
context.canonical:
The verse at the centre, Genesis 15:6, comes at the end of a night scene in which a childless old man is shown the stars. It is a verse that joins believing and reckoning in one sentence, and the Old Testament comes back to the idea. Psalm 106:31 uses the same reckoning of righteousness for Phinehas, which shows that a credited righteousness could also follow a zealous deed, and that is why Paul must read Genesis 15 in its own context and not by the pattern of that later verse. Nehemiah 9:8 remembers that God found Abraham's heart faithful. Isaiah 41:8 calls him God's friend, and James 2:23 repeats that title.

The New Testament uses Abraham in three ways. Paul, here and in Galatians 3:6-9, makes him the father of all who believe, and Galatians 3:17 adds that the law, which came 430 years later, cannot cancel a promise made before it. James reads the same verse and holds that his faith was seen in the offering of Isaac, James 2:21-24. Hebrews 11 praises his faith as an act of trust in the God who can raise the dead, Hebrews 11:17-19, and notes that Sarah too considered Him faithful, Hebrews 11:11.

David's blessing in Psalm 32:1-2 is the second witness. It sits in the great penitential psalms, where a king who knows his own guilt calls the forgiven person blessed. The chapter then points forward to Isaiah 53 and the cross: the Servant 'was delivered over' for our sins, Isaiah 53:12, and in 4:25 Paul says Jesus was delivered over for our trespasses. The thread from Genesis to the gospel is tied tight in this one chapter.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul wants his readers to understand that the gospel is not an innovation. A skeptic in Rome could say that justification by faith alone was a clever new teaching designed to make room for Gentiles, and Paul answers by going to the founding document of the Jewish faith and showing that the founder was justified in exactly that way. The chapter is an argument from Scripture, meant to persuade people who hold Scripture as final.

He also intends to reframe what faith is. In some minds faith was a kind of loyalty that, once exercised, entitled one to a reward. Paul insists that faith is the opposite of earning. In verses 4 and 5 he sets the wage-earner against the one who simply believes, so that faith means giving up any claim and receiving. The portrait in verses 18 to 21 then fills out what such faith looks like in practice: fully aware of the facts, 'the decrepitness of his body' and 'the lifelessness of Sarah's womb,' and yet persuaded that God can do what He has promised.

Last, Paul writes to bring unity. The father of the circumcised and the uncircumcised is one man, and the family is formed by faith. The chapter aims to teach each group in Rome to see the other as part of a single household that God has gathered by His own promise.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter is mostly an interpretation of a story, and it states its own application in verse 23: 'the words it was credited to him were written not only for Abraham, but also for us.' That is a rare moment of Paul telling his readers how to read narrative, and it is worth heeding. The story of Genesis 15 is not just history. It shows the pattern of how God accepts people, and that pattern is for every believer.

At the same time, not everything in the Abraham narrative is a model. He misjudged God's timing and took Hagar, Genesis 16, and he laughed in unbelief at the promise of a son at ninety, Genesis 17:17, although Paul's portrait emphasises his faith and passes over these lapses. The point is that the faith credited to him was not flawless performance. It was trust in the promise. That guards against two errors. One treats Abraham as a moral hero who earned approval. The other reads his story as permission to be careless. Paul's description of faith as being 'fully persuaded that God was able to do what He had promised' gives the pattern. The believer is invited to rest in God's promise in spite of visible evidence, and to give glory to God in doing so.

debates.question: Does Paul contradict James, who says Abraham was justified by works?

views.label: Different questions, one gospel
views.case: Both writers cite Genesis 15:6, but they answer different questions. Paul asks how a sinner is accepted by God and says faith alone, apart from works. James asks what kind of faith is real, and says it is a faith that works, as Abraham's did when he offered Isaac, James 2:21-22. Paul uses 'justify' for God's declaration of acceptance. James, on this reading, uses it for the demonstration of genuine faith in front of others. The faith that justifies is never alone.

views.label: A different target
views.case: Others notice that James attacks a claim to faith without any deeds, James 2:14-17, while Paul attacks a claim to be accepted on the strength of deeds. Each is guarding against a different distortion, and neither is asserting the opposite of the other. Verse 22 of James, 'his faith was working with his actions,' fits Paul's picture of a faith that does not stay inert.

views.label: A real tension that Scripture leaves
views.case: A few readers see a sharper disagreement, and think the two authors carry different emphases that cannot be fully harmonised. They argue that it is better to let each speak than to flatten them.

debates.bearing: The first two views agree on the main point and are supported by the text. Justification is a gift received by faith alone, and the faith that receives it is alive. Paul guards the freeness of grace and James guards the reality of faith.

debates.question: Are the 'works' Paul excludes moral achievement, or the boundary markers of Jewish identity?

views.label: Works as human merit, the traditional reading
views.case: The Reformers read 'works' as any effort to earn standing before God. Verses 4 and 5 support this, since they use wages and obligation, which is the language of earning, and verse 2 speaks of boasting. The question of the whole letter is how a guilty person can be right with God, 3:19-20, and the answer is that no effort will do.

views.label: Works as the markers of Jewish identity
views.case: Some modern scholars argue that the 'works of the law' in this context chiefly means circumcision, the Sabbath and the food laws, the badges that separated Jew from Gentile. They point out that verses 9 to 12 are about circumcision and that the whole letter is about uniting two peoples.

views.label: Both together
views.case: A third approach holds that Paul's argument covers both: the Jewish markers were the form that the temptation to boast took, and the underlying problem was pride in one's own standing, whatever its form. Romans 3:27-28 and 4:4-5 together cover the whole range.

debates.bearing: Paul clearly attacks ethnic boasting, but verses 4 and 5 go beyond it to the heart of the matter. Even a person who has no badge to display is justified only as a sinner receiving a gift.

debates.question: What does it mean that faith is 'credited' as righteousness?

views.label: Righteousness imputed from outside
views.case: The Reformation reading takes the accounting language at face value. God credits righteousness that is not the believer's own to his account, grounded in the work of Christ and received through faith. The contrast with wages in verse 4 and the picture of God justifying the ungodly in verse 5 support this, as does 5:19, where many are made righteous through the obedience of one.

views.label: Faith itself is the thing counted
views.case: Others read the verse to say that God graciously accepts faith in the place of perfect obedience. Faith is treated as if it were righteousness, though it is not the same thing.

views.label: Faith as the means of covenant membership
views.case: Another reading takes the verse chiefly as a declaration of who belongs to God's people, with faith as the sign. The righteousness in view is the status of being in the right with God.

debates.bearing: The language of verses 4 to 8 fits best with a righteousness that comes from God and is received by faith, not earned by it. The accounting terms say that a gift is added to the ledger, and that a debt is cancelled.

study.originalLanguages:
The word that carries the chapter is logizomai, 'to credit' or 'reckon,' and it is worth watching how it is used. It occurs eleven times in verses 3 to 24. It is a word of accounting that can also mean to conclude or reckon, as in Romans 3:28, and Paul sets three uses against one another. Verse 4 contrasts a wage reckoned as a debt, verse 5 a faith reckoned as righteousness, and verse 8 a sin not reckoned at all. The Hebrew behind Genesis 15:6 is chashab, and Paul follows the Greek translation, which uses the same verb. In Romans 6:11 he will use the same verb for believers to 'count' themselves dead to sin, so that credited righteousness and reckoned death belong together.

The second word is the verb 'believe' in Genesis 15:6, from the Hebrew aman, the root of 'amen.' To believe in this sense is to take something as firm and reliable, to lean on it. It is not mere mental agreement. The promise in Genesis 15 was that Abraham's offspring would be like the stars, and the narrator says he leaned on the LORD.

In verse 5 Paul says God 'justifies the ungodly,' ton asebe. The word asebes means the irreverent, someone with no regard for God, and it is the word used in 5:6 of the ones for whom Christ died. Read beside Exodus 23:7 and Proverbs 17:15, the phrase is shocking. Judges in Israel were forbidden to acquit the guilty, yet God does it, and the next chapter will show how the cost is borne.

Verse 11 calls circumcision a 'sign' and a 'seal.' Semeion, sign, points to something beyond itself, and sphragis, seal, is the stamp that authenticates and secures a document. Circumcision did not make Abraham righteous. It confirmed in his body a righteousness he already possessed by faith.

Verse 15 says 'where there is no law there is no transgression.' The Greek word for transgression, parabasis, means a step across a line, which requires a line to be drawn. Sin is present before the law, as Romans 5:13 says, but the law marks it as breach.

Verse 17 describes God as the one who 'gives life to the dead' and 'calls into being what does not yet exist.' The Greek is zoopoieo, to make alive, and a phrase that says God calls things that are not as though they were. This is the language of creation, and it ties the promise of a child to the first chapters of Genesis.

Verse 18 has a deliberate paradox, par' elpida ep' elpidi, 'against hope, in hope.' Against all natural expectation, Abraham held to hope in God. Verse 19 says his body was 'as good as dead,' a perfect participle, nenekromenon, describing a settled condition. Verse 20 says he 'was strengthened' in faith, a passive verb, endynamothe, which suggests that the strength came to him as he gave glory to God, and verse 21 says he was 'fully persuaded,' plerophoretheis, a word of being filled to the brim with conviction, the same word used of settled conviction in Romans 14:5. Finally, verse 25 says Jesus was 'delivered over' for our trespasses, a phrase that many hear as an echo of Isaiah 53:12, and 'for' in the Greek, dia with the accusative, is used twice in parallel, for our trespasses and for our justification.

typology.type: Abraham as father of many nations, Genesis 17:5
typology.fulfillment: God changed Abram's name to Abraham, 'father of many nations,' while he still had one son by a servant and no heir by Sarah. The promise looked absurd. Paul reads it as a promise that reaches its true size when Gentiles join the family by faith, Galatians 3:7-9. In Christ, the one offspring through whom all nations are blessed, Galatians 3:16, the promise is fulfilled in a family that no one can count. The type falls short in that Abraham fathered a people by birth, while Christ gives a family by new birth.

typology.type: Isaac's birth from a dead womb and his return from the altar
typology.fulfillment: Abraham and Sarah received a son when their bodies were as good as dead, and Hebrews 11:17-19 adds that Abraham reasoned God could raise Isaac from the dead, and in a sense he received him back. Paul sees in this the shape of the resurrection of Jesus, verses 17 and 24. The escalation in Christ is that He was not spared at the altar but actually died, Romans 8:32, and was actually raised. The type falls short in that Isaac was a substitute provided, Genesis 22:13, while Jesus is the substitute.

typology.type: Circumcision as sign and seal, Genesis 17:10-11
typology.fulfillment: Circumcision marked the body as belonging to the covenant. Paul explains that it sealed a righteousness already received, verse 11. In Christ the sign is turned inward, as the prophets had hoped, Deuteronomy 30:6 and Jeremiah 4:4, and Colossians 2:11-12 describes a circumcision not made by hands, joined to burial and resurrection with Him. Philippians 3:3 says believers are the true circumcision. The type falls short because the physical sign could be given to anyone, whether or not he believed, while the circumcision of the heart is the work of the Spirit.

typology.type: The offering of the only son, Genesis 22:16-18
typology.fulfillment: The angel's oath praised Abraham because he had not withheld his only son, and promised that all nations of the earth would be blessed through his offspring. The echo in Romans 8:32 is hard to miss: God 'did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all.' The father who was ready to give his son is a faint shadow of the Father who did. The shadow falls short because God stopped Abraham's hand, while the Father did not stop the cross.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ by three roads, and the first is the promise itself. Everything God said to Abraham, a land, a great name, countless descendants, blessing for all nations, was aimed at a single descendant. Paul says it plainly in Galatians 3:16: the promise was spoken 'to Abraham and to his seed,' meaning one, who is Christ. So when Romans 4 says the promise would be heir of the world, verse 13, it is looking toward the one who inherits all things and shares His inheritance with His people. Christ is the heir who makes Abraham's family worldwide.

The second road is faith's object. Abraham believed in the God who gives life to the dead, verse 17, and Paul says that believers believe in the same God, 'Him who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead,' verse 24. The structure is intentional. The shape of Abraham's faith, trust in a God who brings life from deadness, is the shape of Christian faith, and the resurrection of Jesus is the final and greatest case. Romans 1:4 says Jesus was declared Son of God in power by His resurrection, and Paul now says that the same event is the ground of justification.

The third road is the last verse. 'He was delivered over to death for our trespasses and was raised to life for our justification.' The parallel is balanced and deliberate. Christ was delivered up for the sake of our sins, and raised for the sake of our justification, which is to say that the verdict of acquittal rests as much on His resurrection as on His death. His death paid the debt, and His resurrection is God's public declaration that the debt is cleared and that the one who took it on has been accepted. Without the resurrection there would be no proof that the payment was received, 1 Corinthians 15:17. The phrase 'delivered over' recalls Isaiah 53, where the Servant is made an offering for sin and justifies many.

David's psalm also points forward. The man whose sin is not counted against him is blessed, Psalm 32:1-2, and the reason such a person can be blessed is that his sin has been counted somewhere else. Isaiah says the LORD laid on the Servant the iniquity of us all, Isaiah 53:6, and that is where the uncounted debt goes.

A caution is in order. It would be forced to turn every detail of the Abraham story into an allegory of Christ, such as the number of years or the names of his servants. The links that carry weight are those the New Testament itself draws: the single seed, the resurrection faith, the offering of the son, and the blessing of the nations.
study.god:
This chapter shows God as the one who gives, who promises, and who keeps His word. The first thing it says about Him in verse 5 is that He justifies the ungodly, and the verb tells us that God does not begin where we expect. He does not first look for people who have made themselves ready. His gracious action is directed at people with no standing at all. The question of how God can do this without becoming unjust has already been answered in 3:25-26, and so chapter 4 can rest in the plain fact of it.

God is the creator who calls into being what does not exist. Verse 17 sets the promise of a child for the old couple in the same category as creation out of nothing. The God of Genesis 1, who spoke and it was so, is the same God who speaks to Abraham. That gives faith its ground. It does not rest on Abraham's strength, on the likelihood of the promise, or on his reading of his circumstances. It rests on who God is. The same attribute is behind the resurrection, which is why the final verses can run from Abraham's old body to the empty tomb without strain.

God is also faithful and powerful. Verse 21 says Abraham was fully persuaded that God was able to do what He had promised. Ability and promise are joined here, as they are throughout Scripture. A promise from a person who cannot perform it is wishful, and power without a promise offers no hope. In God both are present, and so the believer can trust. Numbers 23:19 and Titus 1:2 speak in the same vein of a God who does not lie.

Verses 6 to 8 show His mercy. The forgiven person is called blessed, and his sin is not counted against him. The same God who keeps strict accounts in verse 4 refuses to count the sins of the one who trusts. His justice and His mercy are not at odds, and verse 25 will place the cost where it belongs.

God is further shown as the God of both circumcised and uncircumcised, who deals with each by the same principle. His promise in Genesis 12:3 reached all the families of the earth, and verse 16 says that it was meant 'to all Abraham's offspring.' For worship, the lesson is that the life of faith is a life of glory given back to God, verse 20. Abraham 'gave glory to God' precisely by believing, because to doubt a promise is to question the one who made it, and to trust it is to honour Him. Praise and trust turn out to be the same act.

crossReferences.note: The night scene behind Paul's quotation. Abram, old and childless, is told to count the stars. The verse before the quotation shows what he believed: that the offspring would come from his own body, not from a servant. Paul's chapter turns on this, that the credit follows the promise and not any act of Abram's.

David's song after confessing sin. Paul quotes it as a second witness to a righteousness credited apart from works. The one who is blessed is the one whose transgressions are forgiven and whose sin is not counted, which shows that forgiveness and credited righteousness describe the same gift.

God renames Abram as Abraham, for he has been made a father of many nations. Paul quotes it in verse 17 and sets it in the presence of God. The renaming shows that the promise was spoken about a future the old man could not see.

Circumcision is given as a sign of the covenant, and the order matters: the sign comes after the promise and after the credit of Genesis 15:6. Paul's argument in verses 9 to 12 rests on this sequence, which shows that circumcision seals faith and does not create it.

A parallel argument in a letter written to a different crisis. Those who have faith are sons of Abraham, and the Scripture 'foretold the gospel to Abraham.' It shows that Paul's reading of Genesis was not a one off but his steady teaching, and it adds that the blessing of the nations is already in Genesis 12.

James reads the same verse and ties it to the offering of Isaac. Its mention that the faith was 'working' with the works shows that James is describing living faith, while Paul describes how it is credited. Read together the two passages show that the faith that justifies is the faith that acts.

Sarah, as well as Abraham, is praised for considering God faithful, and the descendants come from one man 'as good as dead.' It uses the same word for deadness that Paul uses in verse 19, and shows how the early church read the story as a lesson in resurrection faith.

After the offering of Isaac, God swears by Himself that He will bless Abraham, multiply his descendants, and bless all nations through his offspring. It joins the promise to the obedience of faith, and Paul's later phrase in Romans 8:32 echoes its language about not withholding a son.

The same reckoning of righteousness is used of Phinehas after his zeal at Peor. It shows why Paul must read Genesis 15 on its own terms. Here the credit follows an act, while in Abraham's case it followed a promise believed, with no deed yet done.

The righteous Servant justifies many by bearing their iniquity, and is numbered with the transgressors. The last verse of Romans 4 uses the same pair: delivered over for trespasses, raised for justification. It tells us where the sins that are not counted against the believer have been counted.

study.oneStory:
After the fall, the human story is a story of people trying to get back to God by their own hand: a fig leaf, a tower, a name. Genesis 12 turns on a different pattern. God speaks first and calls a man out of an idolatrous family with a promise that all the families of the earth will be blessed. Abraham's response is to believe, and the verse that tells it, Genesis 15:6, is the quiet centre of the whole Old Testament's account of how people come to God.

The Old Testament then watches that promise pass through a series of impossibilities. A barren wife, Hagar and Ishmael, the offering of Isaac, the famine, the slavery in Egypt, the exile, each time the promise looks closed, and each time God opens it. Paul reads all of this as a single line that leads to the seed who is Christ, and to a family that is formed not by birth but by faith.

Romans 4 is where the line becomes visible. Abraham believed the God who gives life to the dead, and a people of that same belief are now gathered from every nation. The covenant sign changes from circumcision to baptism and Spirit, the land promise widens to the world, verse 13, and the offspring become as countless as the stars. The same thing that began with one old man under the stars is now a worldwide church.

The story is still moving. The promise of Genesis 12:3 reaches its goal in Revelation 7:9, where a multitude from every nation, tribe, people and language stands before the throne, and in Revelation 21 where the nations walk by the light of the city of God. The father of many nations has become the father of a multitude no one can number. In that new creation the thing that counts is what counted at the beginning, a person trusting the God who raises the dead, and receiving in Christ the inheritance that could never be earned.

quiz.q: According to verse 3, how was Abraham counted righteous?

options.text: He believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness.
options.note: Paul quotes Genesis 15:6: righteousness came by faith, not works.

options.text: By a mixture of faith and his obedience to God's commands.
options.note: Faith is the way, but Paul excludes works entirely; the worker earns a wage, while Abraham simply believed.

options.text: By his works, which gave him something to boast about before God.
options.note: Verse 2 denies this: even if justified by works he could not boast before God.

options.text: By being circumcised as a sign of the covenant.
options.note: The crediting came before circumcision, as verses 9 to 11 show.

quiz.q: Why does Paul stress that Abraham was justified before he was circumcised?

options.text: So that he is the father of all who believe, both uncircumcised and circumcised.
options.note: The timing makes Abraham father of believing Gentiles and Jews alike.

options.text: To show that circumcision no longer had any meaning for Israel.
options.note: Circumcision was a seal of righteousness already had by faith, not meaningless, but it was never the ground.

options.text: To prove Abraham was actually a Gentile.
options.note: Abraham was the forefather of Israel; the point is the order of faith before circumcision.

options.text: Because circumcision came only later under Moses.
options.note: Circumcision was given to Abraham himself; Paul's point is that faith preceded it.

quiz.q: How does Paul describe the faith of Abraham in verses 18 to 21?

options.text: Against all hope he believed in hope, fully persuaded God could do what He promised.
options.note: His faith trusted the life-giving God despite his and Sarah's deadness.

options.text: A faith that never faced any doubt or obstacle at all.
options.note: He faced the deadness of his body and Sarah's womb, yet did not waver in unbelief.

options.text: A faith based on visible evidence that a son was already coming.
options.note: There was no natural evidence; he trusted the promise, not sight.

options.text: A confidence in his own strength to father a child.
options.note: He acknowledged his body was as good as dead and trusted God, not himself.

quiz.q: What does verse 25 say about the death and resurrection of Jesus?

options.text: He was delivered over for our trespasses and raised for our justification.
options.note: His death answers our sin and His resurrection secures our acquittal.

options.text: He died as an example of faith for us to imitate.
options.note: His death does move us, but it was for our trespasses, a substitution, not merely an example.

options.text: He was raised so that we could follow Abraham's works.
options.note: He was raised for our justification, grounding righteousness by faith, not works.

options.text: His death and resurrection matter mainly for Israel.
options.note: Verse 24 says it is credited to all of us who believe, Jew and Gentile.

quiz.q: What is the difference Paul draws between the worker and the believer in verses 4 to 5?

options.text: The worker is paid a wage as an obligation, but the believer's faith is credited as a gift.
options.note: Grace and wages are opposites; righteousness is credited, not earned.

options.text: Both receive the same reward, whether they work or believe.
options.note: Both do receive something, but Paul contrasts them: a wage is owed, while righteousness is a free gift.

options.text: The believer must first work and then also believe.
options.note: Paul speaks of the one who does not work but believes in Him who justifies the ungodly.

options.text: The worker earns a righteousness superior to the believer's.
options.note: No one is justified by works; the believer receives righteousness by grace.

questions: Abraham was justified not by working but by believing Him who justifies the ungodly. How does it change your standing before God to know that righteousness is credited as a gift and not earned as a wage?
Paul says the words it was credited to him were written for us too. How does reading Abraham's story as your own story strengthen your assurance today?
Against all hope Abraham believed in hope, fully persuaded God could keep His promise. Where are you tempted to weigh the deadness of your circumstances rather than the power of the promising God?
Abraham gave glory to God as he grew strong in faith. How is trusting God's promise itself a way of honoring Him, even before you see the answer?
Jesus was delivered for our trespasses and raised for our justification. How does resting on His finished work, rather than your performance, free you to face your failures this week?

translationNotes.note: Credited renders logizomai, an accounting term meaning to reckon or put to one's account; it recurs eleven times in the chapter and is the key to Paul's argument that righteousness is entered on the believer's account as a gift.
The point is that the crediting of righteousness applies now to all who trust the God who raised Jesus.
